questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 1: before fitting a regression, a clerk plots case duration against claim amount and sees a curved cloud. What should be done first?

options.text: Investigate the non-linear pattern and consider a transformation before fitting a straight line.
Fit a straight line anyway because regression handles curves automatically.
Remove the curved points as outliers.
options.misconception: treats a real pattern as outliers

options.text: Switch to a chi-square test because the data are curved.

questions.explanation: A curved cloud suggests a non-linear relationship. Investigating and transforming before fitting a line avoids a misspecified model.
questions.hint: Address curvature before fitting a line.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The residual as a vertical distance
questions.stem: File note 2: in a regression of case duration on claim amount, what is a residual?

options.text: The horizontal distance between observed and fitted values.
The vertical distance between the observed and fitted values.
The slope of the fitted line.
The intercept of the fitted line.

questions.explanation: A residual is the vertical distance y - yhat. It measures how far an observation falls from the fitted line.
questions.hint: Residual is vertical distance.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 3: why does least squares minimise the sum of squared residuals rather than the sum of raw residuals?

answer.exemplar: Squaring residuals penalises large errors more, avoids cancellation of positive and negative residuals, and yields a closed-form solution for the slope and intercept.

questions.explanation: Raw residuals sum to zero for any line through the means, so they cannot guide fitting. Squaring gives a differentiable, unique solution.
questions.hint: Raw residuals cancel; squares do not.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The slope as a ratio of spreads
questions.stem: File note 4: in a regression of recovery amount on claim amount, the slope is 0.3. What does it mean?

options.text: Recovery increases by 30% on average.
options.misconception: treats slope as a percentage change

options.text: Claim amount explains 30% of the variance in recovery.
For each additional dollar of claim amount, predicted recovery increases by 0.3 dollars.
The correlation between the variables is 0.3.

questions.explanation: The slope is the change in predicted response per unit change in predictor. R-squared, percentage change, and correlation are different quantities.
questions.hint: Slope is change in predicted y per unit x.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 5: a regression of case duration (days) on claim amount has intercept 5. What does the intercept represent?

options.text: The duration added to every case regardless of claim.
options.misconception: treats intercept as a fixed add-on

options.text: The average case duration across all cases.
The minimum possible case duration.
The predicted case duration when claim amount is zero, if zero is within the data range.

questions.explanation: The intercept is the predicted response at x = 0. It is meaningful only if x = 0 is a plausible value within the data range.
questions.hint: Intercept is predicted y at x = 0.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 6: which interval is wider, the prediction interval for a new observation or the confidence band for the mean response?

options.text: The confidence band, because it covers all x values.
The prediction interval, because it includes both uncertainty in the mean and individual variability.
They are equal because both use the same standard error.
options.misconception: thinks the intervals share the same error

options.text: The prediction interval, but only when n is small.

questions.explanation: A prediction interval adds the variability of individual observations to the uncertainty in the mean, so it is always wider than the confidence band for the mean.
questions.hint: Prediction interval includes individual variability.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what R-squared does not imply
questions.stem: File note 7: a regression of case duration on claim amount has R-squared = 0.81. Which statement is NOT justified?

options.text: The fitted line fits the data reasonably well.
options.misconception: states a true interpretation as the unjustified one

options.text: Claim amount explains 81% of the variance in case duration.
options.misconception: states a true interpretation as the unjustified one

options.text: Claim amount causes case duration to change.
There is a strong linear association.
options.misconception: states a true interpretation as the unjustified one

questions.explanation: R-squared measures explained variance and fit, not causation. A high R-squared does not imply that changing the predictor changes the response.
questions.hint: R-squared does not imply causation.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 8: why does adjusted R-squared penalise adding predictors?

answer.exemplar: Adjusted R-squared decreases when a new predictor adds less explanatory power than expected by chance, penalising model complexity.

questions.explanation: Unlike R-squared, adjusted R-squared accounts for the number of predictors, so irrelevant predictors lower it.
questions.hint: Adjusted R-squared penalises unnecessary predictors.

questions.stem: File note 9: a residual plot shows a U-shaped pattern. Identify the problem.

options.text: The R-squared is too high.
The residuals are normally distributed, which is good.
The sample size is too small.
options.misconception: blames n for a systematic pattern

options.text: The linear model is misspecified; a non-linear term or transformation is needed.

questions.explanation: A systematic U-shape in residuals indicates the linear model misses a non-linear component. A transformation or polynomial term is needed.
questions.hint: Systematic residual pattern means misspecification.

questions.stem: File note 10: residuals fan out as claim amount increases. What remedy is appropriate?

options.text: Remove the high-claim cases to fix the spread.
options.misconception: discards data instead of modelling spread

options.text: Apply a transformation such as log of the response or use weighted least squares.
Add more predictors until the fan shape disappears.
Switch to a chi-square test because variance differs.

questions.explanation: Fanning residuals indicate heteroscedasticity. A transformation or weighted least squares stabilises variance.
questions.hint: Transform or weight to stabilise variance.

options.text: A quadratic term may be needed because the relationship is not linear.
A straight line is fine because regression averages curves.
The U shape means there is no relationship.

questions.explanation: A U-shaped pattern indicates a non-linear relationship. Adding a quadratic term captures the curvature.

questions.stem: File note 12: residuals from a monthly case-count regression show a repeating wave. What is suspected?

options.text: Multicollinearity, because predictors are correlated.
options.misconception: confuses time correlation with predictor correlation

options.text: Heteroscedasticity, because variance changes over time.
Autocorrelation, because residuals are correlated over time.
Outliers, because the wave is unusual.
options.misconception: treats a systematic wave as outliers

questions.explanation: A repeating wave in time-ordered residuals suggests autocorrelation. Time-series methods or lag terms address it.
questions.hint: Time pattern in residuals suggests autocorrelation.

questions.stem: File note 13: covariance(x,y) = 24, variance(x) = 8. What is the least-squares slope?
questions.explanation: Slope = covariance(x,y)/variance(x) = 24/8 = 3.
questions.hint: Divide covariance by variance of x.

Because the slope is unknown.
A new observation adds individual variability on top of uncertainty in the mean.
Because R-squared is always low.

questions.stem: File note 24: a confidence band for the mean response is narrowest at which x value?

options.text: It is constant across all x.
At the largest x, because more data are there.
At x = 0, because the intercept is known.
options.misconception: thinks the intercept is known exactly

options.text: At x = xbar, because uncertainty in the mean is smallest at the centre.

questions.explanation: The confidence band for the mean is narrowest at x = xbar, where the line is best determined, and widens toward the extremes.

questions.stem: File note 25: a 95% prediction interval for a new case is (5, 15). What does this mean?

options.text: The mean response is between 5 and 15 with 95% confidence.
About 95% of new observations at this x are expected to fall in this interval.
There is a 95% chance the true slope is in this interval.
95% of the data lie between 5 and 15.

questions.explanation: A prediction interval captures where a new individual observation is expected to fall, not the mean, slope, or data range.
questions.hint: Prediction interval is for a new individual.

A new observation at x = 10 will fall between 8 and 12.
options.misconception: confuses confidence band with prediction interval

options.text: We are 95% confident the true mean response at x = 10 lies between 8 and 12.
The slope is between 8 and 12.

questions.explanation: A confidence band for the mean captures the true mean response at a given x, not a new observation or the slope.

questions.stem: File note 27: in a log-log model, the slope is 0.5. What does it represent?

options.text: The correlation is 0.5.
A 1-unit increase in x multiplies y by 0.5.
options.misconception: treats slope as a multiplier on raw x

options.text: y increases by 0.5 units per unit of x.
A 1% increase in x is associated with a 0.5% increase in y.

questions.explanation: In a log-log model, the slope is an elasticity: a 1% change in x associates with a slope% change in y.
questions.hint: Log-log slope is an elasticity.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 28: a predictor measured last month explains this month's case count better than this month's value. What is this?

options.text: A spurious relationship, because time is involved.
A lagged relationship, where a past value of the predictor predicts the response.
Autocorrelation, because the response is correlated with itself.
Heteroscedasticity, because variance changes over time.
options.misconception: mislabels a lag effect as variance change

questions.explanation: When a past value of a predictor predicts the current response, the relationship is lagged. This is distinct from autocorrelation of the response.
questions.hint: Past predictor value predicting current response is lagged.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 29: two trending series both rise over time and show a high R-squared when regressed, but neither causes the other. What is this?

options.text: Autocorrelation of residuals, which is harmless.
A strong causal relationship proven by high R-squared.
Spurious regression due to shared trends rather than a true relationship.
Heteroscedasticity, because trends increase variance.
options.misconception: mislabels a trend problem as variance

questions.explanation: Shared trends can produce high R-squared without a true relationship. Detrending or cointegration analysis addresses spurious regression.
questions.hint: Shared trends can fake a relationship.

questions.topic: A curve hidden by a high fit
questions.stem: File note 30: a linear model has R-squared = 0.95, but the residual plot shows a clear curve. Identify the problem.

options.text: The sample size is too large.
The model is fine because R-squared is high.
The residuals are too small to matter.
High R-squared can mask a misspecified functional form; the model should be revised.

questions.explanation: A high R-squared does not guarantee correct specification. A curved residual pattern means the functional form is wrong.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.stem: File note 31: a treatment looks better in each subgroup but worse overall. What is this?

options.text: A calculation error, because totals must agree with subgroups.
options.misconception: thinks aggregation cannot reverse a comparison

options.text: Simpson's paradox, due to unequal subgroup sizes or confounding.
Multicollinearity, because subgroups are correlated.
Heteroscedasticity, because subgroup variances differ.

questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox occurs when an association reverses upon aggregation, often due to confounding or unequal subgroup sizes.
questions.hint: Aggregation can reverse an association.

questions.topic: Odds ratios for a binary outcome

options.text: The probability of disease doubles for the exposed group.
The odds of disease are twice as high for the exposed group.
The relative risk is 2.0.
options.misconception: confuses odds ratio with relative risk

questions.explanation: An odds ratio of 2 means the odds of disease are doubled for the exposed. It is not a probability, rate, or relative risk.
questions.hint: Odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities.

questions.explanation: Measurements within a case are correlated, so the effective sample size is smaller than 100. Ignoring clustering understates standard errors.

questions.stem: File note 34: a risk score predicts 30% probability but the actual event rate is 10%. What is the issue?

Poor calibration, because predicted probabilities do not match observed rates.

questions.explanation: Calibration compares predicted probabilities to observed rates. A mismatch indicates poor calibration, distinct from ranking ability.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The cost of a data leak
questions.stem: File note 35: a model uses a variable recorded after the outcome to predict it, yielding high accuracy. What is the issue?

options.text: Overfitting, because the model is too flexible.
High accuracy, which is always desirable.
Data leakage, because the predictor is not available at prediction time.
Multicollinearity, because predictors are correlated.

questions.explanation: Data leakage uses information unavailable at prediction time, inflating accuracy unrealistically. The model will fail in production.
questions.hint: Leakage uses future information.

questions.topic: A fit value that hides a curve

The arch is normal and can be ignored.

questions.explanation: R-squared alone can mask misspecification. Residual plots reveal curvature that R-squared does not.

questions.stem: File note 37: residuals increase in spread as the predictor increases. What is this called?

questions.explanation: Increasing residual spread indicates heteroscedasticity, a violation of constant variance. Homoscedasticity is the opposite.
questions.hint: Non-constant variance is heteroscedasticity.

questions.explanation: A small standard error means the slope estimate is precise. It does not imply the slope is zero or fit is perfect.

questions.learningObjective: State the null for a slope test
questions.stem: File note 50: what is the null hypothesis in a test for the slope?

options.text: H0: R-squared = 0.
H0: beta1 != 0, a linear relationship exists.
